--- title: Designing view transitions description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. nav_title: View transitions --- In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. ## Add view transitions with an agent The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app. Install the skill: ```bash filename="Terminal" npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-view-transitions ``` Then prompt the agent with something like: ```prompt Add view transitions to this app using the vercel-react-view-transitions skill. ``` Or prompt for a specific transition, such as: - Morphing a thumbnail into a hero image - Sliding between routes forward and back - Crossfading content within the same route To apply the patterns yourself, follow the walkthrough below. ## Example As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). You can find the resources used in this example here: - [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) - [Code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo) View transitions work in the App Router with no configuration. events.content:
View transitions are wired up across the gallery using React’s `<ViewTransition>` component and the patterns from the [Next.js view transitions guide](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/view-transitions).

### Shared element morph (grid → detail)
Product thumbnails and detail hero images share a `name` (`product-${slug}`) with `share="morph"` so the image morphs between grid and detail views.

### Directional page navigation
- Product links use `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`
- Back link uses `transitionTypes={['nav-back']}`
- Page content is wrapped in `PageTransition` for horizontal slide animations

### Suspense skeleton → content
Skeleton fallbacks use `exit="slide-down"` and loaded content uses `enter="slide-up"` on both the home grid and product detail info.

### Reduced motion
`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` disables view transition animations and skeleton pulse effects.

### Dependency update
React was upgraded to `19.3.0-canary` because `ViewTransition` isn’t available in React 19.2 stable yet.

**Files changed:**
- `app/PageTransition.tsx` — reusable directional page wrapper
- `app/page.tsx` — page transitions + Suspense reveals
- `app/ProductGrid.tsx` — shared element names + forward navigation
- `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` — hero morph, back navigation, detail Suspense reveals
- `app/globals.css` — transition keyframes and reduced-motion rules
- `package.json` / `package-lock.json` — React canary for `ViewTransition`
